short: The waterway that tied the rice of the Yangtze to the armies and capitals of the north.
full:
Emperor Yang of Sui ordered the main works in 605. The Tongji Canal joined the Yellow River to the Huai and on to the Yangtze; the Yongji Canal, dug from 608, ran north towards the site of modern Beijing; a southern extension reached Hangzhou. Older Han and Warring States channels were absorbed into the system. Contemporary accounts put the conscripted workforce in the millions and the deaths in the hundreds of thousands, and the resentment it caused contributed directly to the rebellions that destroyed the dynasty that built it.

It worked, though, and that decided Chinese geography for a thousand years. The economic centre of the country had shifted south to the Yangtze while its political and military centre stayed north, and the canal was the only way to move grain between them in bulk. The Yuan rerouted it in the 1280s to run directly to Beijing, shortening it to about 1,800 kilometres. Silted sections were still being dredged in the twentieth century, and parts remain in commercial use.
